lesson_title: Tins of Beans and the Acid Test: Liquidity, Solvency and the Owner's Return
hook_text: You can't pay the rent with tins of beans. That's a real accounting ratio.
clip_script: Every family knows the month-end test. The bills queue at the door — rent, electricity, the school transport money. On the table: this month's incoming money, the tins stacked in the cupboard, the money your uncle still owes you. Can what is coming in cover what is knocking? Business calls that the current ratio. But a careful gogo sharpens it: 'the cupboard counts, yes — but I cannot pay the rent with tins of beans.' Set the stock aside — tins still need a buyer — and ask again with only the near-cash things. THAT is the acid test. Then the bigger, quieter question for hard seasons: if we had to settle everything by selling everything, would there be enough? Solvency. And finally the owner's own question: my money lived in this shop all year and earned forty-two percent — the bank pays seven. Worth it? Almost — but the bank's seven is promised, and the shop's forty-two was sweated for. Risk deserves its wage. Three household questions. Three famous ratios. Same test.
visual_style: A kitchen table at month-end: bills stacking at the door, resources laid out and sorted; a tin of beans greying out for the acid test; the whole house weighed on a scale for solvency; two jars — bank 7% vs shop 42% — for the finale.
mood: Grounded, familial, quietly empowering — accounting as street wisdom.
pacing: Three-act structure, one question per act, tightening to the risk-deserves-its-wage punchline.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run all three tests on a real business.
